Patient & GP Details

Clinical Assessment

Identified Problems/Provisional Diagnoses:
- Principal: Suspected acute uncomplicated cystitis (urinary tract infection) — High likelihood (clinician impression and DDx concordant)
- Secondary: Urethritis due to sexually transmitted infection (Chlamydia/Gonorrhea) — Medium likelihood (DDx; consistent with sexual history and absence of prior STI screen)
- Tertiary: Urolithiasis (lower urinary tract stone) — Low–Medium likelihood (DDx)

- Medications: Recently tried over-the-counter bicarbonate (ineffective). Antibiotic prescribed (either Nitrofurantoin or Trimethoprim) — regimen stated as one tablet twice daily for three days; exact agent selected not documented.

Risk Assessment:
- Suicidal/Self-Harm/Risk to Others: No suicidal ideation, self-harm intent, or risk to others reported.

Formulation:
- Predisposing factors: Young female, sexually active, no prior STI screening.
- Precipitating factors: Several days of dysuria with suprapubic cramping, malodorous urine and an episode of visible hematuria.
- Perpetuating factors: Continued sexual activity (advised to avoid while symptomatic), absence of prior STI screening, lack of immediate diagnostic testing documented (no urine dip/culture, NAAT or pregnancy test recorded).
- Protective factors: Prompt help-seeking behavior, social support from flatmates and partner, clinician engagement and safety-netting.
- Integrative statement: The patient presents with an acute, likely uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection causing mild situational anxiety and embarrassment. Differential includes urethritis from STI (medium likelihood) and less likely urolithiasis; absence of systemic features reduces likelihood of pyelonephritis at this time. Management priorities are empiric antibiotic treatment, symptomatic care, STI risk assessment/testing as indicated, and safety-netting for progression to upper tract infection.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Suspected acute uncomplicated cystitis
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Rapid symptom relief (reduced dysuria and suprapubic pain).
  - Avoid complications (kidney infection).
  - Minimize interruption to study/social life.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Eradicate lower urinary tract infection and reduce symptoms.
  - Monitor for signs of ascending infection; ensure appropriate follow-up/testing as needed.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Take prescribed antibiotic as instructed (one tablet twice daily for 3 days; exact agent not documented).
  - Increase fluid intake to flush urinary tract.
  - Avoid sexual intercourse while symptomatic (clinician advised).
  - Seek review if symptoms worsen or do not improve by end of week.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Provide empiric antibiotic therapy (Nitrofurantoin or Trimethoprim — regimen documented as one tablet twice daily for three days; specific agent chosen not documented).
  - Provide advice on hydration and symptomatic measures (cranberry juice mentioned as possibly helpful).
  - Safety-net: advise return/call if fever, flank/back pain, or clinical worsening (signs consistent with ascending infection).
  - Recommend pregnancy test if clinically indicated/if patient concerned (clinician advised considering pregnancy test).

Secondary Problem: Possible urethritis / STI (Chlamydia/Gonorrhea)
- Patient Goal(s):
  - Obtain STI screening and appropriate treatment if positive.
  - Prevent transmission to partner.
- Clinical Goal(s):
  - Perform NAAT testing for Chlamydia and Gonorrhea (urine or swab as per local protocol); treat if positive; facilitate partner notification if required.
- Actions (Patient):
  - Agree to STI testing if offered.
  - Abstain from sexual activity or use condoms until cleared/treated.
  - Inform partner if diagnosis is confirmed and follow partner notification guidance.
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  - Offer and arrange NAAT testing (urine or cervical/vaginal swab) and consider urine culture if clinically indicated.
  - Provide STI counseling, testing logistics, and partner notification advice.
  - Document test orders/results and follow-up plan (not documented in transcript).

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered:
  - Nature of likely diagnosis (simple UTI), expected antibiotic course, importance of fluids.
  - Advice to avoid sexual activity while symptomatic and to continue barrier contraception when resuming.
  - Use of cranberry juice as symptomatic adjunct (clinician mentioned).
  - Warning signs and when to seek urgent review (fever, flank/back pain, increasing unwellness, failure to improve).
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening:
  - Development of fever, flank or back pain, vomiting, marked worsening of symptoms, persistent hematuria, or lack of improvement by end of week.
- Coping Strategies:
  - Hydration, rest, prompt contact with GP if symptoms worsen, clear communication with partner regarding symptom avoidance of sexual activity until resolved.

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Yes — patient verbally agreed to treatment and follow-up plan during consultation.
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: Not recorded.
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: Not recorded.
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not recorded.
- Review Date: Safety-netting: patient advised to call or return if not improved by end of week; no specific follow-up appointment date documented.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Acute uncomplicated cystitis — High likelihood. Rationale: Young sexually active female with several days of dysuria, suprapubic crampy pain, malodorous urine and an episode of visible hematuria; clinician and DDx concordant.
- Urethritis due to STI (Chlamydia/Gonorrhea) — Medium likelihood. Rationale: Sexually active, never screened for STIs, dysuria may represent urethritis; requires NAAT testing to exclude.
- Urolithiasis (lower urinary tract stone) — Low–Medium likelihood. Rationale: Hematuria and lower abdominal pain could represent a stone, but absence of severe colicky flank pain and systemic features makes this less likely.

Quality checks

  - Vital signs (temperature, pulse, BP) not recorded.
  - Physical examination findings not documented (abdominal exam, pelvic exam).
  - Urine testing (dipstick, microscopy) and urine culture results not recorded.
  - STI testing orders/results not documented.
  - Pregnancy test result not recorded.
  - Exact antibiotic agent chosen (Nitrofurantoin vs Trimethoprim) not documented.
  - Formal mental health history, structured MSE, and psychiatric risk screening not documented.
  - Specific follow-up appointment date not documented.
- Internal conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None significant; clinician impression in transcript aligns with DDx ranking acute uncomplicated cystitis as most likely.
- Transcript quality notes:
  - Overall dialogue audible and coherent; occasional brief inaudible/overlapped phrases noted. No physical exam or diagnostic test data included in transcript.
